job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6)

Below are the issues I found, in section order. The most serious ones are the sunset in §7(b), the exemption in §3(c), and the unenforceable registry in §4. A priority list follows the numbered items.

1. **§2(1)(A), volume threshold:** Operators can split activity across several vessels, each under 10,000 metric tons per year, or set up affiliated entities to stay below the cap. "Per year" and "recovery" are also unmeasured (wet or dry weight, and how sediment discharged without recovery is counted). Fix by aggregating across all vessels and affiliates under common control, and by defining the measurement.

2. **§2(1)(A), depth floor:** The 200-meter minimum excludes shallower seabed mining, such as continental-shelf and EEZ operations, from the definition. Remove the floor or cover all seabed recovery above a set volume.

3. **§2(1)(A), "mineral resources":** The term is undefined and could be read to exclude seabed massive sulfides, cobalt-rich crusts, phosphorites, rare-earth muds, or sand and aggregate. Define "seabed mineral resources" broadly.

4. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** The bill doesn't say which Secretary (Commerce/NOAA or Interior), and it sets no criteria, procedure, deadline, or notice requirement for the "comparable risk" determination. The catch-all depends entirely on agency discretion, which makes it hard to enforce and easy to challenge in either direction. Name the agency, set criteria, and require rulemaking.

5. **§2(1)(B) and §3(a), "engage in":** The term is undefined, so financing, insuring, chartering vessels, supplying equipment, and directing operations may fall outside the prohibition. Define "engage in" to cover these activities.

6. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition excludes foreign-incorporated subsidiaries and US-controlled foreign entities, and it may not reach LLCs or partnerships. "State" is also undefined (does it include DC, Puerto Rico, or the territories?). Extend the definition to entities controlled by US persons and to US-organized LLCs and partnerships, and define "State."

7. **§2(3), "covered vessel":** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold and the phrase "equipped for" leave out smaller vessels, barges, towed or seafloor collectors, and modular systems. "Vessel" is also undefined. Remove the tonnage threshold or make it operational, and define "vessel" to include platforms, collection systems, and support craft.

8. **§3(a), territorial reach:** "In the United States" doesn't say whether it includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the outer continental shelf. Foreign persons operating foreign-flagged ships in international waters are also outside the prohibition. Define the geographic scope and consider a flag or registration condition.

9. **§3(a), no import or commerce ban:** Minerals mined by foreign or unregistered operations can still enter the US market, which weakens the prohibition's practical effect. Add a prohibition on importing, selling, or processing unlawfully recovered materials.

10. **§3(b), grandfathered exploration licenses:** "Exploration license" and the issuing authority are undefined, and there are no limits on volume, duration, renewal, transfer, or conversion to commercial recovery. The phrase "mining conducted under" could be read to permit full commercial operations. Limit the exemption to exploration activities with volume caps and an expiration date, and bar transfer and renewal.

11. **§3(b), enactment cutoff:** Tying the grandfather date to enactment invites a rush to obtain licenses before the bill passes. Move the cutoff to the date of introduction or the markup.

12. **§3(c), environmental-assessment exemption:** The exemption is undefined and has no permit requirement, volume cap, duration limit, or bar on selling recovered material. A company could label commercial recovery as "assessment." Require a Secretary-issued permit, cap tonnage at test-sample levels, bar sales beyond testing, and require public notice and reporting.

13. **§3, §5(a), and §8, timing conflict:** §5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the prohibition's effective date by 180 days. It's unclear whether conduct in that window is penalized. Align the penalty trigger with the effective date.

14. **§4(a), scope of registration:** "Operator" is undefined, and registration applies only to covered vessels, so operations using smaller vessels escape the registry. No registration deadline is set. Define "operator" to include owners, charterers, and controlling entities, extend registration to all vessels engaged in seabed recovery, and set a deadline.

15. **§4 and §5, no penalty for registry violations:** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failure to register or file a report carries no sanction. Add penalties for violations of §4, including false certifications.

16. **§4(b), report content:** Quarterly reports have no required content (volumes, locations, depths, sediment-plume monitoring, discharge data), and "certified by the operator" carries no false-statement liability. Specify required contents, require environmental monitoring data, make reports public, and attach liability for false statements.

17. **§5(a), missing enforcement tools:** The bill names no enforcing official and gives no authority to seek injunctions, issue cease-and-desist orders, seize vessels or minerals, or forfeit proceeds. It also has no citizen-suit provision. Add these tools.

18. **§5(a), penalty calculation:** Per-day penalties are hard to prove for vessels in international waters or for continuous operations. The penalty has no inflation adjustment and no mechanism for recovering ecosystem restoration costs. Consider per-ton or per-vessel-day penalties, add inflation adjustment and cost recovery, and include a presumption that violations continue.

19. **§5, individual and secondary liability:** The bill has no provisions for officers, directors, financiers, aiding and abetting, or attempted violations, so corporate structures could shield the people who direct operations. Add these provisions.

20. **§5(b), "willfully":** The term is undefined, which invites a narrow reading of criminal intent. Define it, or specify the knowledge standard.

21. **§6, treaty obligation:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no concrete duty, no report to Congress, and no consequence if negotiations fail. "Equivalent" is also undefined. Require a report to Congress, define equivalence, and set a review or extension trigger if no agreement is reached.

22. **§7(a), reversal standard:** "Serious harm" and "can be conducted without serious harm" are undefined, the NAS report has no deadline or scope, and there's no expedited procedure for the joint resolution. The reversal path is also hard to evaluate in litigation. Define the standard, set a deadline and scope for the NAS report, and specify the criteria Congress must apply.

23. **§7(a) and §7(b), internal conflict:** §7(a) makes the prohibition indefinite, but §7(b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect after 10 years. A court would have to reconcile these, and the likely result is that the ban expires. Delete the sunset or convert it to a review requirement. This is the most important fix in the bill.

24. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The bill doesn't say whether penalties, pending enforcement actions, or existing violations survive the sunset. Add a savings clause.

25. **§8, transition:** The bill has no wind-down rules for operations already underway or for vessels in the middle of a campaign. Set a limited transition for permitted activity with a fixed end date.

26. **Missing severability clause:** If a court strikes a provision (for example, the vague delegation in §2(1)(B)), the whole Act could fall. Add a severability clause.

27. **Missing relation-to-other-law clause:** The bill doesn't address the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (1980), under which NOAA already issues licenses and permits, or the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. It also doesn't address preemption of state law. Add a clause on the relationship to existing law and on preemption, and have counsel confirm the interaction with DSHMRA and OCSLA.

28. **Missing rulemaking and appropriations authority:** The Secretary has no explicit authority to issue regulations under §2(1)(B) or §4, and there's no funding for NOAA's registry or enforcement. Add both.

29. **Missing findings and purpose section:** Without findings, courts have little guidance on how to read "comparable," "serious harm," or the scope of the prohibition, which weakens the bill's defensibility. Add a findings section.

30. **§3(a) and §6, extraterritorial reach:** Reaching US persons abroad is generally supportable, but the bill doesn't address conflicts with ISA-sponsored contracts or with foreign-flagged operations. Have counsel review the foreign-relations and international-law exposure before markup.

---

**Priorities for Thursday:**

1. Fix the §7(a)/§7(b) conflict (item 23).
2. Close the §3(c) exemption (item 12) and the §3(b) grandfather (items 10–11).
3. Make the §4 registry enforceable (items 14–16).
4. Add enforcement tools and penalties (items 17–19).
5. Address the import and commerce gap (item 9) and the scope definitions (items 1–8).

**Caveats:** I've flagged these based on the text alone. Before filing amendments, have Hill counsel confirm the jurisdictional points (NOAA, BOEM, and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee's role under OCSLA) and check the committee's deadline for filing amendments before the October 15 markup.
